topic: Sound for Picture — Post Workflow & Deliverables

flags: No attested, canonical meaning for 'Age matching' in sound-for-picture post workflow or deliverables. The voice-casting practice of matching a dub actor's vocal age to a character exists but is not defined under this name in acceptable sources (Yewdall 'The Practical Art of Motion Picture Sound', Holman 'Sound for Film and Television', Rose 'Producing Great Sound for Film and Video'; SMPTE/EBU delivery standards; manufacturer technical docs), and it is not a transparent audio-technique compound. All fields left blank pending clarification of intended sense.

fields.definition: A Foley performance style in which everyday sync sound effects — footsteps, cloth, and prop handling — are performed with heightened force and energy so they read louder, sharper, and more physically emphatic against the picture.
fields.plain_english: Foley is when an artist makes body and prop sounds in time with the picture. Aggressive Foley just means playing those sounds hard and loud, so a punch or a stomp feels big and forceful.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to give action physical weight and impact, so hits, footsteps, and movement feel powerful and believable instead of soft or lost in the background.
fields.practical_application: A Foley artist uses it on fights, chases, and horror beats — stomping harder and striking props firmly — and the mixer then rides the level to match the on-screen energy.
common_mistakes: Trying to fake it by only raising the fader in the mix instead of actually performing the movement with more force.
Overplaying every action so quiet scenes lose contrast and the track becomes tiring to listen to.
Not matching the performance to the character's weight, surface, and footwear seen on screen.
scenario_contexts: Cutting Foley for a hand-to-hand fight so each punch and body fall lands hard.
Building footsteps for a heavy, angry character storming through a room.
Adding forceful cloth and prop sounds to a tense action beat.

sources: Vanessa Theme Ament, 'The Foley Grail: The Art of Performing Sound for Film, Games, and Animation'
David Lewis Yewdall, 'The Practical Art of Motion Picture Sound'

fields.definition: The subtle, low-level sound of moving air — drafts, ventilation, wind, or the wash created by a body or object passing the camera — added to a soundtrack to convey open space, motion, or a living environment rather than dead silence.
fields.plain_english: Air movement is the soft sound of air on the move, like a breeze, a vent, or the wind when someone runs past. Editors add it so a scene feels alive and open, not empty and dead.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to give a scene a sense of space and presence and to smooth over gaps, so quiet moments still feel natural instead of unnaturally silent.
fields.practical_application: An editor lays a faint air or wind bed under exteriors and large spaces, or drops in a small air whoosh as a character or object sweeps past frame.
common_mistakes: Setting the level too high so the air bed pulls attention away from dialogue.
Using a looped air sound with an obvious repeat or audible seam.
Confusing air movement with room tone, which is the still, steady sound of a specific interior.
scenario_contexts: Adding a faint breeze bed under a wide outdoor shot.
Placing an air whoosh as a car speeds past frame.
Filling a large hall with a soft moving-air presence.

sources: David Lewis Yewdall, 'The Practical Art of Motion Picture Sound'

fields.definition: A dialogue or performance edit in which a word, line, or phrase from a different recorded take is cut in to replace or improve the matching moment in the chosen take, blended to match its timing, tone, and background.
fields.plain_english: Actors usually record a line many times. An alternate-take edit means swapping in a word or line from one of those other tries to get a cleaner read, then blending it so no one hears the join.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to fix problem words — noise, flubs, or weak reads — without re-recording, by borrowing the best moments from other takes of the same performance.
fields.practical_application: A dialogue editor auditions the alternate takes, finds a clean version of a troublesome word, cuts it into the main take, and smooths the edit with matching room tone and crossfades.
common_mistakes: Cutting in an alternate take whose background or mic tone does not match, so the join is audible.
Ignoring lip sync when the alternate word has different timing than the picture.
Forgetting to fill the edit with matching room tone, leaving a hole in the sound.
scenario_contexts: Replacing a word ruined by a cough with the same word from another take.
Swapping in a stronger read of a key line without calling the actor back for ADR.
Fixing a plosive or noise on a single word using a clean alternate.

sources: John Purcell, 'Dialogue Editing for Motion Pictures: A Guide to the Invisible Art'

fields.definition: A defined region of a scene or space assigned its own ambient sound bed, so that as the picture or listener moves between areas the background changes to match each location's character.
fields.plain_english: An ambience zone is an area given its own background sound. Move from a busy street into a quiet shop, and the ambience zone changes the background so each place sounds right.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to keep backgrounds believable across a scene, giving each space its own sonic identity and smooth transitions as the story moves between areas.
fields.practical_application: An editor maps different ambiences to zones — a lobby, a kitchen, an alley — and crossfades between them as the camera or character crosses from one to the next.
common_mistakes: Cutting hard between zones instead of crossfading, so the change sounds abrupt.
Making every zone equally loud, which loses the contrast between spaces.
Forgetting to shift the ambience when the picture clearly changes location.
scenario_contexts: Changing background sound as a character walks from a party into a bathroom.
Assigning distinct ambiences to rooms in a house for a walk-through scene.
Transitioning from interior to exterior ambience through a doorway.

sources: Audiokinetic Wwise Documentation (Ambiences and spatial ambience design)
David Lewis Yewdall, 'The Practical Art of Motion Picture Sound'

fields.definition: A section of ambient or background recording edited to repeat seamlessly, used to sustain a continuous environmental sound over a duration longer than the original recording.
fields.plain_english: An ambient loop is a background sound, like rain or a busy room, edited so it can play over and over with no gap. It lets a short recording fill a long scene without you hearing it restart.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to provide continuous, gap-free background for a scene of any length from a limited recording, saving time and keeping the environment consistent.
fields.practical_application: An editor finds matching in and out points, crossfades the ends, and loops the clip across the whole scene, checking that no click or obvious repeat gives the loop away.
common_mistakes: Choosing a clip with a unique sound, such as a car horn, that gives away the repeat.
Leaving a click or level jump at the loop point.
Making the loop too short, so the repeating pattern becomes obvious.
scenario_contexts: Looping a short rain recording to cover a long dialogue scene.
Sustaining crowd ambience under an entire restaurant sequence.
Filling a forest exterior with a seamless nature bed.

sources: Audiokinetic Wwise Documentation (Looping ambient sounds and blend containers)

fields.definition: A defined relationship showing how a signal's level is reduced as a function of another variable — most often distance in spatial audio, or frequency in a filter — expressed as a curve rather than a single fixed amount.
fields.plain_english: An attenuation curve is a graph of how much a sound gets quieter as something changes, like how a sound fades the farther away it is. It sets the rule for how fast the level drops.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to control level change in a smooth, predictable way, so sounds fall off naturally with distance or a filter rolls off gently across frequency.
fields.practical_application: In spatial or game audio, an editor shapes the distance attenuation curve so a source fades realistically as it moves away; in an EQ, the curve describes how much each frequency is cut.
common_mistakes: Confusing attenuation, which reduces level, with gain, which raises it.
Using a curve that drops too fast, so sources vanish unnaturally quickly.
Assuming attenuation only means volume and ignoring filtering across frequency.
scenario_contexts: Setting how a sound source fades with distance in an immersive mix.
Shaping a filter's roll-off across frequency.
Adjusting a fall-off curve so a passing vehicle recedes smoothly.

sources: Audiokinetic Wwise Documentation (Distance-based attenuation and attenuation editor)

fields.definition: Any discrete piece of audio content — a recording, sound effect, music cue, or edited clip — managed as a named, reusable file within a project, media library, or deliverable package.
fields.plain_english: An audio asset is any single piece of sound in a project, like one sound effect, a music track, or a recorded line. Each one is a file you can name, store, and reuse.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to treat sound as organised, trackable items, so material can be found, shared, versioned, and delivered reliably across a production.
fields.practical_application: An editor imports, labels, and organises assets in the session and media pool, then hands off the required assets as part of the final deliverable package.
common_mistakes: Leaving assets with default or unclear names, making them hard to find later.
Delivering a session that points to assets that were never included or consolidated.
Forgetting to keep metadata with the asset, which loses key information about it.
scenario_contexts: Organising sound effects in a library for a project.
Consolidating every clip so the session's assets travel with the deliverable.
Tracking versions of a music cue as separate assets.

sources: Avid Pro Tools Reference Guide (clips, media, and session data management)
Tomlinson Holman, 'Sound for Film and Television'

flags: 'Audio behavior' is an abstract phrase, not a defined term in sound-for-picture or game-audio literature, and not a transparent compound of an established technique plus a source/section. No acceptable source (post-production texts such as Yewdall/Holman/Rose, SMPTE/EBU delivery standards, or audio-middleware technical documentation) defines it as a distinct term. All fields left blank pending clarification of intended sense.
